questions.question: You have 5 minutes to (a) decide if an article is worth reading and (b) find the year a bridge was built. Which strategy fits each?
questions.solution: (a) SKIMMING — read titles, first/last sentences for the gist. (b) SCANNING — hunt for the specific datum (a year) without reading everything. Skimming takes the text's shape; scanning targets a fact. Choosing the right strategy for the purpose is the core reading skill.

questions.question: In a paragraph about traffic congestion in Kathmandu, which sentence is the main idea and which are details? How do you tell?
questions.solution: The main idea is the sentence the others EXIST to support — usually the topic sentence ('Traffic congestion has become the city's most urgent problem'). Details (specific jams, statistics, examples) elaborate, prove or illustrate it. Test: if you removed a sentence, would the paragraph's point survive? Details can go; the main idea cannot.

questions.question: 'Rita checked her watch for the third time and edged toward the door.' What can you infer, and why is inference different from stating a fact?
questions.solution: Inference: Rita is impatient, wants to leave, perhaps has an appointment. The text never SAYS this — the reader combines clues (repeated watch-checking, edging) with knowledge of human behaviour. Inference = evidence + reasoning beyond the literal words; it must stay anchored to textual evidence, not free invention.

questions.question: How can you tell whether a passage aims to inform, persuade or entertain — and what signals the tone?
questions.solution: Purpose shows in structure and content: inform — facts, definitions, neutral wording; persuade — opinion, emotive words, calls to action; entertain — story, humour, vivid imagery. Tone (serious, ironic, sympathetic) shows in word choice and rhythm. Ask: what does the writer WANT me to do or feel after reading?

questions.question: Why is guessing an unknown word from context often better than stopping to look it up mid-reading?
questions.solution: Context supplies the meaning AND shows how the word is used — its grammar, register and partners — which a dictionary entry alone does not. Stopping breaks reading flow and comprehension of the whole. Best practice: guess from context, confirm later in the dictionary if the word keeps appearing.
